title: LCA of an Electric Vehicle Battery: Critical Raw Materials, Recycling and Second Life
sub: A cradle-to-grave assessment of a 60 kWh NMC811 battery pack, comparing virgin materials, recycled content, low-carbon manufacturing and a second-life scenario.
pdf: Case 07 — LCA of an Electric Vehicle Battery: Executive Summary
fu: One 60 kWh NMC811 lithium-ion traction battery pack providing energy storage over a 200,000 km first vehicle life in Europe
ref: One 400 kg battery pack (≈260 kg cells); battery-attributable charging losses over 200,000 km; end-of-life collection and hydrometallurgical recycling
boundary: Cradle-to-grave for the battery: extraction of lithium, nickel, cobalt, manganese and graphite; refining and cathode/anode production; cell manufacturing; pack assembly; transport; use-phase charging and battery losses; second life (scenario); recycling and recovery of critical raw materials
geo: Raw materials from Australia, Chile, Indonesia, DR Congo and China; cell manufacturing in East Asia (baseline); use and recycling in Europe
time: 2024–2026 technology; 10-year first vehicle life; GWP100 (IPCC AR6)
method: EF 3.1 characterisation; IPCC AR6 GWP100; AWARE for water scarcity; ADP (ultimate reserves) for minerals and metals
alloc: Second-life scenario allocates 75% of production burdens to first life (based on delivered energy throughput); recycled content via cut-off; mining co-products allocated economically
cutoff: Flows <1% of mass and energy excluded (thermal interface materials, labels) with cumulative exclusions <5%; battery management electronics included
dq: Argonne GREET, peer-reviewed battery LCAs, ecoinvent, EU Batteries Regulation targets; no manufacturer data. Overall data quality Medium; Low for mining water and social risks
srcShort: Illustrative model; parameters within ranges from Argonne GREET, Dai et al. (2019), the JRC battery footprint work, ecoinvent and published NMC battery LCAs.
loop: Circular loop: second-life stationary storage, then recycling of nickel, cobalt, lithium and copper into new cathodes
exec:
This case study assesses a 60 kWh NMC811 battery pack for a battery electric car. EV batteries are central to transport decarbonisation and are regulated by the EU Batteries Regulation, which introduces carbon footprint declarations, recycled-content minimums from 2031 and material recovery targets for lithium, cobalt, nickel and copper.
The illustrative baseline result is 5,400 kg CO2e per pack (90 kg CO2e per kWh). Refining and cathode production (25%) and cell manufacturing (23%) are the largest contributors, followed by charging losses attributed to the battery during use. Lithium extraction drives water consumption, and nickel and cobalt processing drive acidification and toxicity.
Recycled content at the 2031 regulatory minimums reduces the result by about 6%. Combining recycled content with renewable electricity for cathode and cell production cuts it by about a third. Allocating part of the burden to a second life in stationary storage lowers the first-life share to about 2,900 kg CO2e, a 46% reduction.
Recommendations focus on low-carbon cell and cathode manufacturing, traceable and responsibly sourced critical raw materials, and designing packs for second life and recycling. For CSRD, results are relevant to ESRS E1, E5 (critical raw materials and circularity), E2, E3, E4, and to S2 and S3 because of human-rights risks in mining.
overview:
A lithium-ion traction battery is assembled from thousands of cells grouped into modules, with a battery management system, cooling and an aluminium or steel housing. NMC811 cathodes contain mainly nickel, with smaller amounts of manganese and cobalt.
The purpose of this LCA is to identify where emissions and resource pressures arise, and to quantify the benefits of recycling, clean manufacturing energy and second-life use for procurement and circular-economy strategy.
goal: The goal is to support a vehicle or battery manufacturer's supply-chain decarbonisation and circular-economy strategy, and preparation for carbon footprint declarations under the Batteries Regulation. The audience is procurement, engineering, sustainability and ESG reporting teams. This is not a declared battery carbon footprint.

stages.what: Mining of nickel and cobalt ores, lithium from brine or spodumene, and natural or synthetic graphite.
stages.in: Ore, brine, diesel, explosives, electricity, water
stages.ew: ≈9,000 MJ; brine evaporation dominates water consumption (≈21,000 L)
stages.tr: Mine to port by truck and rail
stages.so: Child labour and artisanal mining risk (cobalt), Indigenous water rights (lithium brines), deforestation (nickel laterites)
stages.as: Mix of Australian spodumene and Chilean brine lithium; Indonesian and Australian nickel; Congolese cobalt

stages.what: Metals are refined into sulphates and hydroxides, then into precursor and NMC811 cathode active material.
stages.em: CO2 from coal-heavy grids and process heat; SO2
stages.tr: Shipping to cathode plants in East Asia
stages.so: High-pressure acid leaching plants in Indonesia raise environmental and community concerns

stages.what: Graphite anode, electrolyte, separator, copper and aluminium foils, housing and electronics.
stages.in: Graphite, LiPF6, solvents, copper, aluminium, steel

stages.what: Electrode coating and drying, cell assembly in dry rooms, formation and ageing.
stages.ew: ≈25 kWh electricity per kWh of cells
stages.as: East Asian grid 0.8 kg CO2e/kWh in baseline

stages.what: Modules, cooling, battery management system and housing are assembled.
Shipping of cells or packs to Europe.
Battery-attributable energy losses during charging and discharging over 200,000 km.
stages.as: EU grid 0.26 kg CO2e/kWh; vehicle consumption excluded except battery losses

stages.what: Collection, discharge, dismantling, black mass production and hydrometallurgical recovery.
stages.out: Nickel, cobalt, lithium salts, copper, aluminium
stages.wa: Graphite and electrolyte largely lost; residues
stages.as: 95% collected; recovery efficiencies in line with 2031 targets; no credit (cut-off)

hot.t: Refining and cathode production on coal-heavy grids
hot.why: Converting ores into battery-grade nickel, cobalt and lithium compounds is energy- and chemical-intensive; it is the largest stage (25%) and a major source of acidification.
Electrode drying and dry rooms consume large amounts of electricity. On a 0.8 kg CO2e/kWh grid this is 23% of the total.
Lithium brines drive water consumption in arid regions; nickel laterite mining drives deforestation; cobalt carries child-labour risks.
Battery losses over 200,000 km add about 900 kg CO2e on the EU grid, falling as grids decarbonise.

hot.t: Graphite and electrolyte losses in recycling
hot.why: Current recycling recovers metals well but loses most graphite and electrolyte, limiting circularity.

desc: All primary materials; cells made on an East Asian grid
16% recycled cobalt, 6% lithium, 6% nickel, 50% recycled aluminium and copper
As previous, plus renewable electricity for cathode, cell and pack production (e.g., European gigafactory)
As previous, with 8 years of stationary storage after vehicle use; 25% of production burdens allocated to second life

sens.t: Sensitivity: carbon intensity of cell manufacturing electricity
sens.xl: Grid carbon intensity for cell manufacturing (kg CO₂e/kWh)
sens.note: Manufacturing location and electricity source are the most controllable parameters for cell makers.
sens.interp: Moving cell production from a coal-heavy grid to renewable power saves about 1,200 kg CO2e per pack (≈22%). Process innovation matters less once electricity is clean.

ci.stage: Production stages account for over 80% of the battery's life-cycle climate impact; use-phase losses about 17%.
ci.stage_e: Refining and cell manufacturing dominate energy demand.
ci.stage_w: Water consumption is concentrated in lithium extraction, especially brine evaporation in arid regions.
ci.donut: Nearly half the result comes from two process steps (refining and cell manufacturing), typically located in a few countries, which concentrates supplier engagement.
ci.sankey: About 58% of the pack mass is recovered as metals in recycling; graphite and electrolyte are mostly lost.
ci.heat: Extraction and refining are hotspots across water, land, pollution and resources; cell manufacturing is a climate and energy hotspot.
ci.scen: Clean manufacturing energy matters more than recycled content at today's regulatory minimums; second life spreads production burdens over more delivered service.
ci.radar: All improvement scenarios reduce every indicator; second life gives the largest reduction per first-life functional unit.
ci.wf: Clean electricity in manufacturing and refining delivers the largest share of reductions.

interp.m: The battery's footprint is mainly set before the car leaves the factory, in refining and cell manufacturing. Where and how cells and cathodes are made matters more than the vehicle's use.
interp.a: Grid intensity for refining and cells; lithium source (brine vs spodumene); allocation for second life; recycled-content levels; lifetime.
interp.u: Mining water and land data are site-specific; allocation for second life is a methodological choice; future recycling performance is uncertain.
interp.can: Clean manufacturing energy and responsible sourcing are the main levers; recycling and second life improve resource efficiency.
interp.cannot: This study does not compare EVs with combustion vehicles, and cannot verify supplier-specific claims or the social performance of mines.
interp.d: Supplier selection and contract requirements for low-carbon cells and cathodes, recycling partnerships, second-life business models, preparation for battery carbon footprint declarations.

recs: Design packs for disassembly, state-of-health diagnostics and second life; consider chemistries with lower cobalt and nickel (e.g., LFP) where range allows.
Require supplier-specific carbon footprints, renewable electricity in cathode and cell plants, and third-party audited responsible sourcing (e.g., IRMA, RMI).
Locate cell production on low-carbon grids; recover NMP solvent; reduce scrap rates.
For dealers and fleets: offer battery health checks and second-life buy-back programmes.
Scale hydrometallurgical recycling with high lithium and graphite recovery; ensure safe collection logistics.
Prepare data for Batteries Regulation carbon footprint declarations and battery passports; align with ESRS E1 and E5 metrics; report due diligence for critical raw materials.
Support recycling capacity, standards for second-life applications, and transparent supply-chain due diligence.

Physical climate risks
Water scarcity at lithium sites; extreme weather at mines and ports

Recycled content (Co, Li, Ni), recovery efficiencies, second-life share, collection rate
Pollution indicators
SO2 and acid emissions from refining; tailings management

Biodiversity indicators

Social risks

take: An EV battery's footprint is set mainly in refining and cell factories: clean electricity there, plus recycling and second life, can cut its first-life footprint roughly in half.
biz: Make low-carbon cathode and cell production a supplier selection criterion, secure traceable and responsibly sourced critical raw materials, and design packs for second life and high-yield recycling ahead of Batteries Regulation requirements.
assume: NMC811, 60 kWh, 400 kg pack; cell manufacturing 25 kWh/kWh at 0.8 kg CO2e/kWh; 10% battery losses over 200,000 km on the EU grid; 75/25 allocation for second life; cut-off for recycled content. Social risks assessed qualitatively.
